demographics.education: B.A. Fashion Merchandising, minor in Entrepreneurship
demographics.occupation: Founder & CEO of a DTC womenswear brand on Shopify

psychographics.identity: Maya sees herself as a product-first founder who built her brand from a personal frustration: she couldn't find well-fitting workwear that didn't cost a fortune. Fashion is her craft; Shopify is her storefront; technology is the lever she uses to compete with brands 10x her size. She doesn't call herself a 'techie' but she's scrappy — she'll try any tool that gives her an edge.
values: Customer experience over growth hacking — she'd rather have 1,000 loyal customers than 10,000 one-time visitors
Profitability before vanity metrics — her brand is bootstrapped and she intends to keep it that way
Representation matters — her product photography uses diverse models, but she knows it's still a compromise
Pragmatic adoption — she'll invest in tools that prove ROI within a quarter, not experimental tech
psychographics.lifestyle: Maya's week splits between creative direction (mornings, when her eye is fresh), operations (afternoons, when decisions need to be made), and customer support (evenings, because she refuses to outsource the relationship). She's in three Shopify founder Slack groups, listens to DTC podcasts during her morning run, and unwinds by actually wearing her own product — she's her brand's most honest fit tester.
psychographics.aspirations: Maya wants to cross $2M ARR without taking venture capital, build a brand that customers evangelize organically, and prove that independent fashion brands can win on experience — not just price or paid acquisition. In five years, she wants to be the brand that other Shopify founders point to and say, 'They did it right.'
psychographics.community: Shopify entrepreneur Slack communities, DTC Twitter (the indie operator corner, not the VC-growth thread), local Austin retail-founder meetups, and a tight group of three other women founders who trade supplier recommendations and vent about return rates.

challenges.challenge: Fit-related returns are quietly eating her margin
challenges.current_solution: Standard product photography with a size chart and customer reviews mentioning fit
challenges.why_it_fails: Photos show the garment on a model with one body type; size charts are abstract numbers shoppers ignore; reviews are anecdotal and don't apply to the reader's specific body. Maya knows roughly 30% of her returns are fit-related but suspects the real number is higher because customers don't always specify the reason.
challenges.quote: 'Every time I process a return tagged "didn't fit," I know that's a customer who might not come back — and I have nothing better to offer them than a refund.'

challenges.challenge: Shoppers hesitate at the product page and abandon carts
challenges.current_solution: High-quality product photography, 360-degree garment videos, detailed size guides
challenges.why_it_fails: None of these help the shopper answer the question they're actually asking: 'How will this look on me?' The hesitation isn't about image quality — it's about imagination. Maya has invested heavily in product imagery and still sees cart abandonment tied to product pages where fit uncertainty is highest (dresses, fitted tops, pants).
challenges.quote: 'I can show them the dress from every angle, on three different models, and they'll still ask "but will it look like that on me?" I get it — I ask the same question when I shop.'

challenges.challenge: Competitors with better tech are raising shopper expectations
challenges.current_solution: None — Maya hasn't found a Shopify-native virtual try-on tool she trusts
challenges.why_it_fails: Virtual try-on experiences she has seen are either clunky (poor rendering), expensive (enterprise-priced), or require a development sprint she can't afford. She's aware that larger brands are adopting this tech and worries her product page experience is starting to feel dated by comparison.
challenges.quote: 'I know virtual try-on is the next thing. I just need one that actually works on Shopify, doesn't look like a video game, and doesn't require me to hire a developer to set it up.'

challenges.challenge: Model photography is expensive and still doesn't represent her customers
challenges.current_solution: Quarterly photoshoots with 3-4 diverse models, supplemented by customer-submitted photos
challenges.why_it_fails: Even with diverse models, Maya can only show a handful of body types — nowhere near the full range of her actual customers. Each photoshoot costs thousands and ages quickly as inventory turns over. Customer photos help but are inconsistent in quality and coverage.
challenges.quote: 'I spend $4,000 a shoot to show four bodies. My customers have four hundred different bodies. There has to be a better way.'

challenges.challenge: Evaluating new Shopify plugins is a time sink with no guarantee of payoff
challenges.current_solution: Trial-and-error: install, test, uninstall when it doesn't deliver
challenges.why_it_fails: Maya has been burned by plugins that overpromise and underdeliver — slow load times, clunky UIs, poor mobile experiences, or setup processes that assume she has a developer on staff. She's skeptical of anything that claims to boost conversion because she's seen too many that didn't.
challenges.quote: 'I've installed and uninstalled more Shopify apps than I can count. At this point, I need someone to show me it works on a store like mine before I'll even click install.'

positive: Pride — in offering a shopping experience that feels premium and thoughtful, not generic
Relief — from the constant background anxiety of returns eating into her carefully managed margins
Confidence — that her product page answers the shopper's real question before they have to abandon the cart to ask it
Satisfaction — of seeing a customer keep and love a garment they bought with fit confidence
Admiration from peers — being the Shopify founder who 'cracked the fit problem' in her niche
Control — over a previously unsolvable part of her ecommerce operation
negative: Frustration — at losing customers to a solvable problem she can't fix with photography or copy alone
Embarrassment — when a customer posts a fit complaint publicly, undermining the brand she's spent years building
Anxiety — about falling behind competitors who invest in emerging tech while she's stuck optimizing the old playbook
Regret — over returns that could have been prevented, each one a customer relationship damaged
Wasted effort — hours spent on photoshoots, size guides, and customer fit consultations that still don't close the gap
Isolation — feeling like she's solving a technical problem without a technical co-founder or team

salience.product_category: AI virtual try-on for Shopify fashion product pages — a fit-confidence layer that sits between the product image and the purchase decision.
salience.problem_solved: Fashion shoppers cannot confidently assess garment fit from standard product photography. Maya's customers need to see themselves in the garment before they'll commit to a purchase, and Maya needs a solution that doesn't require a development team or a six-figure budget.
salience.one_sentence: Fitcheck lets every shopper see how a garment fits their body before they buy — embedded directly in the Shopify product page, set up in a guided session, not a development project.

points_of_difference: Photorealistic AI try-on that renders garments on the shopper's actual body — not a generic avatar or a warped product photo overlay
Shopify-native integration that doesn't require a developer, custom API work, or theme hacking
Guided merchant onboarding that explains real steps and sets realistic expectations — no aspirational setup timelines
Body realism as a product-design principle — representation is built into the rendering pipeline, not added as a marketing afterthought
Credible fit assessment that communicates what try-on can and cannot prove, rather than fabricating certainty
points_of_parity: Works on standard Shopify product pages without requiring a custom storefront
Reduces fit-related returns by increasing pre-purchase confidence
Monthly or annual subscription pricing that scales with the merchant's store
Mobile-responsive — works where Maya's customers actually shop
Does not require shoppers to create an account or download an app
core_features: Photorealistic virtual try-on rendered directly on the product page
Guided setup session that walks Maya through configuration in hours, not sprints
Performance measurement so Maya can see merchant-specific outcomes before expanding rollout
No-model-needed experience — shoppers use their own photo or measurements, not a library of preset models
Fashion-aware rendering that preserves garment drape, fabric texture, and color accuracy

associated_brands: Warby Parker — pioneered virtual try-on for a category where 'how this looks on me' is the entire purchase decision, and made it feel simple rather than gimmicky
Shopify — the platform that gave independent brands a credible storefront without enterprise ecommerce costs; Fitcheck extends that promise to the fit experience
Stitch Fix — proved that technology and fashion can coexist without either one feeling compromised; Fitcheck brings that same data-informed confidence to the self-service shopping moment
usage_locations: On the Shopify product page — at the exact moment of the purchase decision, between 'I like this' and 'I'll buy this'
On mobile — where the majority of Maya's customers browse and where fit uncertainty is highest because images are smaller
During the consideration phase — when a shopper has browsed, liked a garment, and is deciding whether to add it to cart or keep scrolling
usage_methods: Shopper uploads a front-facing photo or provides basic body measurements — one-time setup, reused across all garments in Maya's store
Try-on renders appear inline on the product page alongside standard product photography — not in a separate tool or popup
Merchant configures garment mapping once during guided setup — Fitcheck handles the rendering pipeline from there

positive: Credible — the try-on render is good enough to make a yes/no fit decision, which is all Maya's shoppers actually need
Easy to install — guided setup means Maya can launch without hiring or pausing her product roadmap
Modern — photorealistic rendering signals that Maya's brand invests in the shopping experience, not just the product
Honest — Fitcheck's communication about what the try-on can and cannot prove builds trust rather than overpromising
concerns: Accuracy risk — Maya will worry that an inaccurate render could create a worse experience than no render at all, eroding trust instead of building it
Page performance — every Shopify merchant fears a plugin that slows down their product page and hurts their Core Web Vitals and SEO
ROI uncertainty — at a subscription price point, Maya needs to see evidence that the tool is reducing returns or increasing conversion before she'll commit beyond a trial
Shopper adoption — Maya will wonder whether her customers will actually use the try-on feature or ignore it like they ignore size charts
judgments.credibility: Fitcheck earns credibility through evidence, not claims. The brand does not publish conversion-rate promises without merchant-specific proof. Instead, it offers a guided setup with measurable outcomes — Maya sees her own data before deciding to expand. This mirrors how Maya runs her own business: trust is built on results, not pitch decks. The brand's commitment to body realism and pragmatic precision signals that Fitcheck understands fashion ecommerce well enough to know what a visual try-on cannot prove — and that honesty is itself a credibility signal.

desired_feelings: Confident — that she has given her shoppers the best possible tool to make a purchase decision
Relieved — that the fit-return problem finally has a practical solution she can implement without a dev team
Smart — that she adopted a technology her competitors haven't yet, giving her brand a genuine edge
In control — of a part of her ecommerce operation that previously felt like an unsolvable cost of doing business
Proud — that her product page experience now reflects the quality of her garments and the thoughtfulness of her brand
feelings.voice: A confident guide who explains the 'why' behind recommendations without jargon. The Sage archetype dominates — Fitcheck speaks with earned authority about garment fit — but the Magician surfaces in moments of delight when a shopper first sees themselves in a garment. The voice respects Maya's business instincts, never condescends to her technical questions, and matches her own pragmatic, evidence-backed communication style.
feelings.tone: Direct and evidence-backed, but warm. Fashion-aware without being trendy. Precise about what Fitcheck can and cannot prove — no aspirational language, no vague promises. The tone says: 'We understand this problem deeply, we built a real solution, and we'll be honest with you about what it does.' Enthusiasm is earned, not performed — Fitcheck gets excited about Maya's results, not its own features.

resonance.why_missed: If Fitcheck disappeared, Maya would lose the only Shopify-native tool that gives her shoppers credible, photorealistic fit preview without requiring a development team or an enterprise budget. She'd be back to standard product photography, size charts that shoppers ignore, and fit-related returns she can't prevent — knowing a better solution existed and is now gone. More than the tool, she'd miss the confidence that her product page experience was genuinely competitive with brands 10x her size.
resonance.mission_alignment: Fitcheck's mission — empowering shoppers to confidently see themselves in every garment — aligns directly with Maya's mission of building a brand where every customer feels seen and valued. When Maya reduces fit uncertainty, she's not just reducing returns; she's delivering on the promise she made when she started her brand: that great-fitting clothes should be accessible, and shopping for them shouldn't require imagination or guesswork.
core_values: Fit truth over fit guessing — Maya built her brand on honest garment construction and real fit; Fitcheck extends that honesty to the digital shopping experience
Merchant-first speed — Maya doesn't have a development team or a six-month implementation runway; Fitcheck's guided setup respects her timeline
Body realism, not body idealism — Maya's customer base spans far more body types than any photoshoot can capture; Fitcheck's rendering pipeline treats that diversity as a product requirement
Pragmatic precision — Maya trusts tools that make evidence-backed claims over tools that make aspirational promises; Fitcheck's communication style mirrors her own decision-making
resonance.why_choose_us: Maya will choose Fitcheck because it's the first virtual try-on tool that speaks her language — it doesn't pitch her like an enterprise SaaS buyer or confuse her with technical jargon. It shows up as a guided setup, not a development project; it measures outcomes she cares about (returns, confidence, conversion) rather than vanity metrics; it's honest about what the try-on can and cannot prove, which paradoxically builds more trust than a tool that overpromises. Fitcheck earns Maya's loyalty the same way she earns her customers' loyalty: by delivering a real, measurable improvement to an experience that previously felt broken.
